notes.meaning: King Xerxes calmed down from his drunken fury and remembered Vashti, her beauty, and the decree made against her. Because Persian law was unchangeable, he could not simply take back his decision. Having recently returned from a failed invasion of Greece, he felt lonely and regretted losing his queen.

The king's personal attendants saw his sadness and quickly suggested a solution. They advised sending royal messengers throughout the empire to search for beautiful young maidens for the king. This plan helped keep the king happy and protected the counselors from Vashti ever regaining power.

The counselors advised the king to appoint officers in every province to gather these young women to the citadel of Susa. They were to be placed in the harem under the care of Hegai, the royal eunuch in charge of the women, to receive beauty treatments. In the Persian court, women lived under tight guard and underwent a long preparation before meeting the king.

The attendant proposed that whichever young woman pleased the king most should be crowned queen in Vashti's place. Xerxes liked the plan and put it into effect right away. Behind this pagan search, God was quietly preparing the way to protect His people.

The narrative introduces Mordecai, a Jewish man living in the fortress city of Susa. He belonged to the tribe of Benjamin and traced his family line back through Jair and Shimei to Kish. His ancestry intentionally echoes the family background of Saul, Israel's first king.

Mordecai's family had been carried away from Jerusalem into Babylonian exile more than a century earlier. The mention of King Jeconiah refers to the exile of Judah's leaders in 597 BC. Mordecai was born and raised in Persia, far from the land of his ancestors.

Mordecai raised his younger orphaned cousin Hadassah, whose Persian name was Esther. She was very lovely, and Mordecai cared for her as if she were his own daughter. Her Hebrew name means "myrtle," a symbol of blessing, while her Persian name means "star."

When the king's royal edict was published, many young women were collected at the palace in Susa under Hegai's supervision. Esther was taken along with them into the royal harem. As an exile living under an absolute ruler, she had no power to refuse.

Hegai was deeply impressed by Esther and treated her with special favor. He quickly provided her with the required beauty treatments and special palace food. He also gave her seven select maidservants and moved her into the finest rooms of the women's house.

Esther did not reveal her Jewish people or family background, because Mordecai had told her to keep it secret. In the Persian capital, revealing her heritage could have brought scorn, hatred, or rejection. God used this careful silence to set the stage for her later work.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars believe Esther and Mordecai compromised their faith by hiding their Jewish identity and ignoring biblical dietary laws in order to blend into Persian court life.

notes.meaning: Every day, Mordecai walked back and forth near the courtyard of the harem to learn how Esther was doing. He showed steady, fatherly care for his adopted daughter despite the palace barriers. Working near the court allowed him to receive occasional news from the eunuchs inside.

Each young woman underwent a full twelve months of beauty preparation before being brought to King Xerxes. She spent six months using oil of myrrh and another six months using fragrant spices and cosmetics. This lengthy process followed the elaborate grooming customs of the royal Persian court.

When her turn arrived to visit the king, each maiden was allowed to take whatever jewelry, clothing, or attendants she wanted. The palace staff gave her anything she asked for to help her look as attractive as possible. This was her one opportunity to catch the king's attention.

A young woman would go to the king in the evening and be moved the next morning to a second harem managed by Shaashgaz. From then on, she remained a secondary wife and could never return to the king unless he personally summoned her by name. Most of these women spent the rest of their lives secluded as virtual widows.

When Esther's turn came to go to the king, she asked for nothing beyond what Hegai, the king's trusted eunuch, suggested. She showed modest wisdom by relying on his knowledge of the king's tastes rather than demanding flashy adornments. Her gentle demeanor and natural beauty won the goodwill of everyone who met her.

Esther was brought into King Xerxes' royal palace in the tenth month, Tebeth, during the seventh year of his reign. This was the winter of 479 or 478 BC, about four years after Vashti's removal. The long gap occurred largely because the king had been away leading his military campaign in Greece.

The king loved Esther more than all the other women, and she won his deepest favor. He placed the royal crown upon her head and made her queen in place of Vashti. God guided the king's heart so that Esther gained the influence needed to rescue her people.

The king celebrated Esther's coronation by holding a great banquet for all his nobles and officials. He also granted a holiday or tax relief across the provinces and distributed lavish royal gifts. This grand celebration publicly confirmed Esther's status as the new queen.

Even when a second group of virgins was gathered, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate. In ancient cities, the gate was the public center where court business was handled and legal matters were decided. Sitting there indicates that Mordecai held an official position in the king's administration.

Esther continued to keep her family and Jewish identity secret, just as Mordecai had instructed. Her royal status did not make her proud, and she remained as respectful and obedient to Mordecai as when he raised her. Her humble silence kept her ready for the moment God would call on her.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: The Greek version of Esther includes extra prayers where Esther explains that she hated her royal crown and kept God's laws in secret, sections accepted as Scripture in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

notes.meaning: While Mordecai was on duty at the palace gate, two royal eunuchs named Bigthan and Teresh grew resentful and plotted to kill King Xerxes. Since they guarded the king's private door, they had easy access to his quarters. God placed Mordecai in the right spot to uncover their murderous plan.

Mordecai discovered the plot and reported it directly to Queen Esther, who then informed the king on Mordecai's behalf. Esther humbly gave Mordecai the credit rather than taking it for herself. This report saved the king's life and created an official record that became crucial later.

The report was investigated and confirmed, and both traitors were impaled on wooden stakes. The entire event was recorded in the king's official daily chronicle. Even though Mordecai was not rewarded right away, God saw that the deed was written down for the right time.
